tier_reason: The vteromero/integer-compression-benchmarks README gov2.sorted table shows Delta+BinaryPacking 2.30 G/s encode / 2.33 G/s decode vs Delta+VariableByte 1.62 / 1.52 and Delta+FastPFor128 615.66 / 615.64 M/s on a Core i7-6700HQ, with public harness code (gov2.cc, intbench.cc). The harness Makefile names g++ with -O3 -std=c++11 but no compiler version, so not A; it is a small (5-star) third-party repo by a competing codec's author, not a well-known suite, so C.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: g++ (version unstated); harness built with -Wall -O3 -std=c++11 per the shootout Makefile; the library is built with its own Makefile (make), whose release flags are -O3 plus optional SIMD flags; the CMake Release build in the README applies only to google/benchmark
corrections.caveats: The shootout's BinaryPacking row is the scalar variant: gov2.cc instantiates SIMDCompressionLib::BinaryPacking<BasicBlockPacker>, not the SIMD packer. All codecs in the comparison (VByte, VarIntGB, FastPFor, BinaryPacking) come from this same library, so the baseline is the library's own VByte/FastPFor implementation, not an outside incumbent. Delta+VarIntGB decodes faster on gov2 (2.97 G/s) than BinaryPacking, and FastPFor128 compresses better (ratio 6.21 vs 5.52). The shootout is by the author of a competing codec (VTEnc); compiler version unstated. The README's '4 billion integers per second / 15 GB/s' claim has no table or methodology. The library overlaps with FastPFor and simdcomp, which are listed separately.

notes: Numbers and ratios check out (derived ratios ~1.4x/~1.5x vs VByte, ~3.7x vs FastPFor128 encode). The SPE papers cited in the README (Lemire and Boytsov 2015; SIMD compression and intersection) might support B but arXiv is blocked here; candidate for a paper-access retier. Metadata confirmed: 447 stars, Apache-2.0, last commit 2026-06-07 (version 0.2.0).

tier_reason: The TurboPFor README tables (labelled 2019.11) list 'StreamVbyte 2019' at 11197/11984 MB/s on ZIPF vs FP_VByte 5200/4268 and 8456/9476 on gov2 vs FP_Vbyte 1888/1980, but give no CPU, compiler or flags next to the tables; the icapp code is public. The repo's own perf table (Apple M4 Max) has no baseline. Numbers without full methodology: C.

corrections.hardware: Not stated for the TurboPFor 2019.11 tables; the README links issue #47 ('Skylake i7-6700 3.4GHz'), but that issue holds a different benchmark (test_collection docs/freqs) and does not tie the ZIPF/gov2 tables to that CPU. Repo's own numbers: Apple M4 Max.
corrections.caveats: Numbers come from the TurboPFor README, written by the author of a competing library (TurboPFor); the tables give no CPU, compiler or flags, and linked issue #47 (October 2019) is a different benchmark whose page states the CPU but no compiler or flags. The table is labelled 2019.11; StreamVByte 3.0.0 (April 2026) differs from the '2019' build. StreamVByte compresses worse than VByte in those tables (10.00 vs 8.17 bits/integer on ZIPF, 11.50 vs 8.96 on gov2). The competitor repo also claims TurboByte is faster than StreamVByte (issue #96). The repo's own M4 Max table (500,000 random integers) has no baseline.

notes: All quoted numbers are on the TurboPFor README and belong to the 'StreamVbyte 2019' rows; derived ratios are correct. The peer-reviewed IPL 2018 paper (arXiv 1709.08990; abstract per search snippet: decoding up to twice as fast as varint-G8IU) could support B, but arXiv and the TELUQ mirror are blocked here; candidate for a paper-access retier. Metadata confirmed: 419 stars, Apache-2.0, last commit 2026-06-07; users list verified in README.

tier_reason: First-party README tables (2019.11) compare TurboPack/TurboPackV/TurboVByte against Simple-8b, FastPFor codecs and VByte variants via the public icapp benchmark, but state no CPU, compiler or flags beside the tables; linked issue #47 is a different benchmark with no compiler or flags. First-party with partial methodology: C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: ZIPF table (100M integers, 2019.11): TurboPack scalar 11694 MB/s encode / 10138 decode vs Simple-8b 848 / 3832; TurboPackV sse 17357 / 12363; TurboVByte 11191 / 10333 vs FP_VByte 5200 / 4268. Ratios (derived from page data): TurboPackV decode ~3.2x Simple-8b, TurboVByte decode ~2.4x FP_VByte. gov2.sorted: TurboPackV 7064 / 10268 vs Simple-8b 836 / 3296 and FP_Vbyte 1888 / 1980. TurboPack compression (25.0%) equals fixed-width packing; Simple-8b is 24.0%, so Simple-8b packs slightly smaller there.
corrections.hardware: Not stated beside the README tables; the README links issue #47 titled 'Skylake i7-6700 3.4GHz gcc 9.2', whose page is a different benchmark (test_collection) and states the CPU but no compiler or flags
corrections.caveats: First-party numbers from the TurboPFor README; tables give no CPU, compiler or flags, and linked issue #47 (October 2019) is a separate benchmark whose page lists the CPU but no compiler flags. Tables are labelled 2019.11 and the code has changed since. Self-reported 'No other Integer Compression compress/decompress faster' is marketing wording. FastPFor-family rows marked (*) use 64Ki blocks. GPL-2.0 (commercial license offered), so copying imposes copyleft.

notes: Record mislabelled TurboPack scalar decode as 8876 (that is TurboFor); corrected to 10138 from the ZIPF table. Other numbers and ratios check out. Metadata confirmed: 848 stars, GPL-2.0, last commit 2026-09-21; Debian Code Search listed as user in README. The README links the ADCS 2016 paper 'In Vacuo and In Situ Evaluation of SIMD Codecs' (dl.acm.org, blocked), a possible B source for a later retier.
